newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Voting begins in Yugoslav elections.
newsitem.headline: Voting begins in Yugoslav elections.

text.p: Polling stations opened on Sunday morning in rump Yugoslavia's federal and local elections, the country's first vote since a peace treaty ended four years of war in the Balkans a year ago.
Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling Socialist party and two allied parties were expected to prevail against an opposition coalition, according to Belgrade analysts and opinion polls.

Milosevic, blamed by the West for plunging old Yugoslavia into conflict, now presents himself as a peacemaker and his three-party alliance made no mention of the wars in Bosnia and Croatia during the campaign.

Although Milosevic is not a candidate in the polls, an election victory for his parties should enable him to push through constitutional change that will allow him to stay in power after his second and final term as Serbian president expires next year.
Diplomats say he will assume the post of federal president after the next federal parliament invests the ceremonial post with strong executive authority.

A team of election observers from the United States and several other states from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) were monitoring voting at some of the 10,000 polling stations in Serbia and Montenegro, the two remaining Yugoslav republics.
Polling stations opened at 7 a.m. (0600 GMT) and were due to close at 8 p.m. (1900 GMT).
Voters will be electing a federal parliament and municipal authorities after a campaign in which the opposition was ignored by state television and radio.

The elections were timed to coincide with the formal lifting of international sanctions against Yugoslavia last month. The sanctions were imposed to punish Belgrade for its role in the Bosnian conflict.
Despite the end of the trade embargo, living standards remain at a low level after plummeting during the war.
State television interviewed pensioners coming out of polling stations on Sunday morning, who all said they hoped the country would soon enjoy prosperity.
The opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition had threatened to boycott the election at one point but withdrew the threat after authorities appointed their representatives to electoral commissions.
Official results are not due before November 7 but the outcome was expected to be indicated early in the week by unofficial returns.
